summary: A local feature on the rising popularity of adventure and obstacle racing in the community, tracing how the first race was organized by Thomas Keller. It covers permits, course design, sponsorship, volunteers, construction, weather contingencies and plans to add more technology. The piece argues these races build fitness and community connection.
one_line: Obstacle racing is booming locally, and organizers, officials, designers and sponsors explain how the first community race was planned and run.
key_facts: The local park was transformed for an adventure and obstacle race, described on September 5, 2023, as a fast-growing fitness trend in the city.
Thomas Keller, a former marathon runner, organized the community's first obstacle race, held on October 2, 2023.
Keller said people want to push themselves but also want it to be "fun, social, and a bit of an adventure."

City official Maria Gonzalez said organizers must show the event won't damage public spaces and has adequate safety measures; Keller's proposal required environmental impact assessments and emergency response plans.
Course designer Julie Nguyen said each obstacle tests a range of physical skills while staying safe and scalable for different fitness levels.
Nguyen's course included an obstacle where participants scaled a wall featuring a mural by a local artist.
Payton Electronics, a regional tech company, sponsored a virtual reality obstacle that became the crowd favorite.
Volunteers, including high school teams, local sports clubs and families, staffed stations and handed out water after an overwhelming response to Keller's call.
The race course was 6 miles long with 25 obstacles, including mud pits and rope climbs.
James Harris of Harris & Sons built the obstacles; setup begins less than 48 hours before the event and involves strict safety checks.
Keller said organizers monitor the weather closely and have contingency plans, since a storm can make obstacles much harder.
Keller plans to integrate more technology in the future, such as live tracking of participants or more interactive obstacles.
Participant feedback leads to adjustments in course design, obstacle variety and the registration process.
Race veteran Tim 'the Tank' Johnson called the events "a communal triumph" where competitors help each other.
